You are a requirements analyst at the start of a software project. Nobody has designed the service yet. Below are the full transcripts of three interviews with its future users: a fleet technician, a dispatcher, and the platform's airspace desk. The transcripts are everything you know about these users and their world.

=== TRANSCRIPTS ===
# Interview — a fleet technician

Interviewer: Can you walk me through an ordinary working day for you, from the moment you start until you finish?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: When you first get to work in the morning, what is the very first thing you do?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: What kind of work do you do on the drones?

Interviewee: I keep drones and charging equipment in working order, which includes adding new drones to the fleet, retiring old ones, and taking drones out of service for repairs and putting them back. I also set up charging pads at my company's sites and send drones to charge. Regulators can ask a company to show how its drones have been looked after.

Interviewer: How do you find out that a drone needs repairs or needs to be sent to charge?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: Who hands work to you, and who do you hand work to?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: What was the worst day you had at work in the last few months, and what made it so bad?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: What happens right after something goes wrong with a drone or a charging pad—what do you need to know?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: Is there anything you check by hand today because you don't trust the information you get?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: What are you afraid a new shared service might do wrong for your work?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: When regulators ask to see how your drones have been looked after, what do you have to show them?

Interviewee: Regulators can ask a company to show how its drones have been looked after. I carry out repairs and servicing on the drones and charging equipment.

Interviewer: When you take a drone out of service for repairs and later put it back, what happens step by step?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: When you set up charging pads at your company's sites, what does that involve?

Interviewee: I set up charging pads at my company's sites. My company has a few dozen of them, and the pads are never lent to another company. I also keep charging equipment in working order.

Interviewer: When you send a drone to charge, how does that work?

Interviewee: I send drones to charge, and I keep the charging equipment in working order. Each company has its own charging pads at its own sites, which are never lent to another company.

Interviewer: What happens when you add a new drone to the fleet or retire an old one?

Interviewee: I add new drones to the fleet and retire old ones, while keeping the drones and charging equipment in working order. My company runs a few hundred drones of several models from different manufacturers. These models differ in their carrying capacity, flight range on a full battery, carried sensors, and charging connector types, which are not interchangeable.

Interviewer: Why does it matter that charging connector types are not interchangeable when you set up pads or send a drone to charge?

Interviewee: My company's drones use several connector types that are not interchangeable. Because of this, it matters for the charging equipment I keep in working order, the charging pads I set up at our sites, and the drones I send to charge.

Interviewer: Do dispatchers or anyone else at your company interact with the drones you look after, or let you know when a drone needs attention?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: What do you have to keep track of when you repair or service a drone?

Interviewee: I carry out repairs and servicing on the drones and charging equipment to keep them in working order. Regulators can ask a company to show how its drones have been looked after.

Interviewer: Where do you set up the charging pads, and what do you need to know about a site when you set one up?

Interviewee: I set up charging pads at my company's sites. Each company has its own charging pads at its own sites, a few dozen of them, and pads are never lent to another company.

Interviewer: Why do a drone's carrying capacity, flight range, and carried sensors matter in your work?

Interviewee: My company runs a few hundred drones of several models from different manufacturers. These models differ in how much they can carry, how far they can fly on a full battery, and which sensors they carry. I add these new drones to the fleet and retire old ones while keeping the drones and charging equipment in working order.

Interviewer: Is anything ever shared between your company and the other drone companies when it comes to drones, charging pads, or maintenance information?

Interviewee: Each company's fleet, jobs, sites, and problems are its own business, and pads are never lent to another company. The only thing companies share is airspace information, because that information comes from the authorities and is the same for everyone.

Interviewer: What happens when a charging pad stops working properly?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: How many drones or charging pads do you look after, and how do you tell one drone from another?

How do you decide which charging pad to send a drone to?

Interviewee: I keep drones and charging equipment in working order for my company, which runs a few hundred drones of several models from different manufacturers. Each company has a few dozen charging pads at its own sites, and I set them up. I do not know how I tell one drone from another or how I decide which charging pad to send a drone to.

Interviewer: Does a charging pad work with all of your company's drone models, or only with certain ones?

Interviewee: My company's drones use several connector types that are not interchangeable. Because of this, it matters which charging connector the drone uses and which equipment I keep in working order or set up.

Interviewer: What information do you look at about a drone or a charging pad when you send a drone to charge?

Interviewee: I send drones to charge, and I keep the drones and charging equipment in working order. Our drones use several connector types that are not interchangeable. I do not know what specific information I look at when I send a drone to charge.

Interviewer: When you take a drone out of service for repairs, what changes about that drone?

Interviewee: I take drones out of service for repairs and put them back. I do not know what changes about the drone itself when I take it out of service.

Interviewer: Is there anything else about your work, your company's drones, or your charging equipment that we haven't talked about yet?

Interviewee: I keep drones and charging equipment in working order, which includes adding new drones, retiring old ones, and taking drones out of service for repairs before putting them back. I also set up charging pads at my company's sites and send drones to charge. Regulators can ask a company to show how its drones have been looked after.

---

# Interview — a dispatcher

Interviewer: Walk me through an ordinary working day for you, from the moment you start until you finish.

Interviewee: I plan and run our flights, and as a licensed dispatcher, I am responsible for each flight by deciding which drone flies along which way and signing off before it leaves. Several of us plan at the same time for the same busy sites and popular drones, and I can call off a flight. Before and outside my control, things happen like loads being ready or not, and drones reaching their points and arriving.

Interviewer: What does the first hour of your shift actually look like, step by step?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: Can you walk me through a specific flight you handled recently, from the moment the job appeared until the drone finished?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: What happens when several of you try to plan for the same busy site or the same drone at the same time?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: Tell me about the worst day you had in the last few months—what happened, and what made it so bad?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: Where do the jobs you plan come from, and who do you hand work off to during a flight?

Interviewee: I don't know where the jobs come from. During a flight, people and devices outside the company report whether the load is ready, whether the drone reaches its points, and when it arrives.

Interviewer: What do you double-check by hand today before signing off on a flight because you don't fully trust the information you're given?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: What are you most afraid a new service might get wrong in your work?

Interviewee: I worry about sudden airspace closures and planned ones coming into force while drones from several companies are already in the air, and these closures are often amended during the day. Radio coverage is patchy around ports, industrial sites, and in bad weather, and battery drains faster in cold and wind than planned. Links used to give instructions to drones and charging equipment are unreliable, so an instruction can get through twice when the sender cannot tell if the first attempt arrived.

Interviewer: Right after something goes wrong with a flight, what do you need to know first?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: When you have to call off a flight, what leads to that decision and who needs to know?

Interviewee: I am a dispatcher, and I can call off a flight. I don't know what leads to that decision or who needs to know.

Interviewer: Who else inside your company do you work with or pass information to before or during a flight?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: What happens when an instruction gets through twice to a drone or charging equipment?

Interviewee: I don't know.

---

# Interview — a member of the platform's airspace desk

Interviewer: Walk me through an ordinary working day at the airspace desk, from the moment you start until you finish.

Interviewee: I keep the shared picture of the airspace, which includes the network of flight corridors between sites, the zones grouping them, and the closures announced by the authorities. The authorities define zones where flying is prohibited, and they announce planned closures with a start and end time, as well as sudden ones that apply at once. These closures are often amended during the day, such as when an area is widened or an end time moves, and a closure can even come into force while drones of several companies are already in the air. When a closure is entered, I want to know how much disruption it caused across customers.

Interviewer: How do closures reach you, and what do you actually do when you enter one?

Interviewee: Closures are announced by the authorities as planned ones with a start and end time, or sudden ones that apply at once, and they are often amended during the day, for example when an area is widened or an end time moves. When a closure is entered, I want to know how much disruption it caused across customers.

Interviewer: Can you walk me through a concrete example of the last time you handled a closure, step by step, from the moment you heard about it to when you finished dealing with it?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: What was the worst day you had in the last few months, and what made it so bad?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: Is there anything in your work today that you check by hand because you do not fully trust it?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: What are you afraid a new service might do wrong for your work at the airspace desk?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: Right after something has gone wrong with a closure or the airspace, what do you need to know?

Interviewee: When a closure is entered, I want to know how much disruption it caused across customers. A closure can come into force while drones of several companies are already in the air.

Interviewer: Who hands work to you during the day, and who do you hand work to?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: What does "disruption across customers" mean to you—what specifically are you looking to see when a closure is entered?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: How do changes to the network of flight corridors or zones happen in your day-to-day work?

Interviewee: I keep the shared picture of the airspace, which is the network of flight corridors between sites and the zones that group them. The authorities define zones where flying is prohibited, and they announce closures. I don't know how changes to the network of flight corridors or zones happen in my day-to-day work.

Interviewer: What happens to the shared picture when an authority amends a closure during the day?

Interviewee: Closures are often amended during the day, for example when an area is widened or an end time moves. A closure can even come into force while drones of several companies are already in the air. When a closure is entered, I want to know how much disruption it caused across customers.

Interviewer: Is there anything about how flight corridors, sites, or prohibited zones interact with the companies' flights that you haven't mentioned yet?

Interviewee: Drones fly along corridors between named sites. Sites have only so many places where drones can take off and land at the same time. Drones fly on their own autopilots, and people on the ground supervise them without steering them with a stick through this service.

Interviewer: What do you know or not know about the individual customer companies' operations when you look at the shared airspace?

Interviewee: The airspace desk works for all customer companies and has no business looking into any one company's operations. Each company's fleet, jobs, sites, and problems are its own business.

Interviewer: You mentioned wanting to know how much disruption a closure caused across customers, while also having no business looking into any one company's operations—how do those two fit together for you?

Interviewee: The airspace desk works for all customer companies and has no business looking into any one company's operations, because each company's fleet, jobs, sites, and problems are its own business. However, when a closure is entered, I want to know how much disruption it caused across customers.

Interviewer: What happens to the corridors, zones, or sites when a closure comes into force?

Interviewee: A closure can come into force while drones of several companies are already in the air. The authorities define zones where flying is prohibited, and they announce closures with a start and end time or sudden ones that apply at once. When a closure is entered, I want to know how much disruption it caused across customers.

Interviewer: Who receives the closure updates or the shared airspace picture once you have entered them?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: Is there anything else you do with the shared picture of the airspace that we haven't talked about?

Interviewee: I keep the shared picture of the airspace, which consists of the network of flight corridors between sites, the zones that group them, and the closures announced by the authorities. Beyond this, I do not do anything else with the shared picture that we have not talked about.
=== END OF TRANSCRIPTS ===

Write the requirements for the service: what it must do, so that a team can build it and anyone can check whether it does. Rest every requirement on what the interviews say.

Write them as a list in YAML, in exactly this format, and nothing else:

```yaml
- id: DR-01
  requirement: >
    one thing the service must do, or must not do, and in which case
- id: DR-02
  requirement: >
    ...
```

Number the items DR-01, DR-02, and so on. Each item states one requirement in plain words.
